scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only

tabs.title: Experimental Interpretation
tabs.description: Evaluate DART and the physical limits of deflection.

tabs.title: Scientific Communication
tabs.description: Apply the text to policy and public risk.

questions.q: What epistemic distinction underpins the writer's criticism of sensational headlines?
choices: A nearby object's physical speed is determined by the news coverage.
Asteroid classification depends exclusively on the public perception of risk.
An uncertain prediction reflects incomplete knowledge rather than random motion.
Orbital uncertainty makes all astronomical forecasts worthless.
questions.explanation: The opening distinguishes physical orbital motion from uncertainty in our knowledge of a trajectory.

questions.q: Why can a calculated impact probability initially rise even as research improves?
choices: Several paths fit sparse data, and later observations change their relative plausibility.
The asteroid's orbit necessarily becomes more dangerous after discovery.
Infrared observations systematically exaggerate asteroid sizes.
Astronomers increasingly favour extreme predictions in later reports.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph explains how a narrowing range of possible trajectories can temporarily yield a higher risk.

questions.q: Which reporting practice would most directly address the author's objection to an isolated risk percentage?
choices: Omit uncertainty until the object becomes a public concern.
Replace numerical figures with dramatic photographs.
Quote only estimates that have already fallen to zero.
Give the estimate's date and the range of plausible outcomes.
questions.explanation: The author criticises reporting a compelling number without its date or uncertainty range.

questions.q: Why is reliably striking an asteroid not the whole deflection problem?
choices: The spacecraft must also transmit television pictures to the public.
The resulting motion must be predicted and independently verified.
The asteroid must be visibly brighter than the target star.
The experiment's success is determined solely by the launch date.
questions.explanation: The writer says target properties, expected orbital change and subsequent observation are all essential.

questions.q: How does ejecta from the Dimorphos impact complicate simple momentum calculations?
choices: It prevented scientists from observing any orbital change.
It showed that Dimorphos was a completely solid boulder.
Material thrown off the body added a substantial extra push.
The debris cancelled the force delivered by the spacecraft.
questions.explanation: Paragraph four says the debris plume amplified the change beyond the spacecraft's momentum.

questions.q: What is the scientific value of Hera following DART?
choices: It can investigate the structure and response of the asteroid system.
It will destroy any remaining hazardous fragments.
It will prove that all asteroid collisions are harmless.
It will replace surveys of near-Earth objects.
questions.explanation: The follow-up mission aims to study the system and constrain physical uncertainties.

questions.q: Why might funding for long-term surveys be harder to attract than support for spectacular missions?
choices: Survey instruments have no role in an eventual emergency.
Mission footage is always more scientifically reliable.
International data-sharing is impossible before an impact.
Their preventive benefits are quieter and less immediately visible.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph contrasts essential surveys and communication with attention-grabbing mission footage.

questions.q: A news outlet calls every orbit revision a scientific embarrassment. What is the writer's likely objection?
choices: An earlier prediction should always remain the official figure.
Revisions supported by new data are part of responsible scientific practice.
Impact probabilities should never be publicly shared.
Scientists must wait for certainty before calculating trajectories.
questions.explanation: The author advocates transparent revisions instead of presenting uncertainty as failure.

questions.q: What would make a planetary-defence warning system publicly credible according to the text?
choices: Clear responsibility for messages and transparent corrections when evidence changes.
A promise that no asteroid can ever reach Earth.
A rule against releasing low-probability estimates.
A single annual announcement regardless of new observations.
questions.explanation: The text calls for institutional clarity and the open correction of conflicting claims.

questions.q: What general scientific principle does the DART evidence illustrate?
choices: One successful mission demonstrates a permanent solution.
The material properties of target objects never matter.
An observed experimental result must be interpreted within its conditions and uncertainties.
An orbit can be predicted perfectly once the spacecraft arrives.
questions.explanation: DART demonstrates a real effect, but transfer to other objects requires physical understanding.
